etymologies.etymologyHTML: 1590s, lug (“to drag”) +‎ -age, literally “that which is lugged, dragged around”. Duplicate -g- is to clarify pronunciation of the vowel ‘u’ (which is pronounced unchanged from lug). Compare baggage.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The bags and other containers that hold a traveller's belongings.

quote.citation: August 4, 1726, Jonathan Swift, letter to Alexander Pope
quote.text: I am gathering up my luggage, and preparing for my journey.

definitions.definition: (countable, nonstandard or obsolete) A specific bag or container holding a traveller's belongings.

quote.citation: 1858, “Letter from Rev. George L. Seymour”, in The African Repository and Colonial Journal, volume 34, page 13:
quote.text: I assisted some time ago in cutting up a tree, that made tolerably good turns or luggage for nineteen or twenty persons, which could be procured for about two dollars at the stump.

quote.citation: 1875, W. G. Willson, Report of the Midnapore and Burdwan Cyclone of the 15th and 16th of October 1874‎[1]:
quote.text: The passengers injured who could not get out were removed out by the railway staff, and then taking part of the luggage the train started back for Burdwan.

quote.citation: 1964 [1957], Colin MacInnes, City of Spades, London: Penguin Books, page 15:
quote.text: Namely, leaving my luggages at the Government hostel, to go straight out by taxi (oh, so slow, compared with our sleek Lagos limousines!) to the famous central Piccadilly Tube station where I took a onestop ticket, went down on the escalator, and then ran up the same steps in the wrong direction.
